text: Right now, your head is ageing faster than your feet. Sounds crazy. But it's true. <#0.3#> In October twenty twenty six, scientists built a brand new kind of clock. To see why it matters, let's go back three hundred years. <#0.4#> Seventeen oh seven. Sailors had a big problem. To know where they were at sea, they needed to know the exact time. <#0.4#> Their clocks weren't good enough. One stormy night, four British warships hit rocks. More than fourteen hundred sailors died. <#0.5#> So a carpenter named John Harrison spent decades building a better clock. At sea for almost three months, it lost just five seconds. <#0.4#> That's the secret of every clock. Something inside it ticks, again and again. The steadier the tick, the better the clock. <#0.5#> Harrison's clock ticked with a little swinging wheel. Today, atomic clocks count the steady wobble of an atom, billions of times every second. <#0.4#> Your phone's map depends on them, up in satellites. Off by just a billionth of a second, and your blue dot moves thirty centimetres. <#0.5#> But atoms have a weakness. Their outer parts get pushed around by heat and magnets. <#0.4#> So in October, two teams, in Vienna and Beijing, built clocks that listen to the atom's tiny core instead. It's better protected. <#0.4#> It's called a nuclear clock. It's not yet better than the best atomic clocks. But it could become around ten thousand times steadier. <#0.5#> Remember your head and your feet? Clocks this good can feel gravity. Time runs faster the higher you go. <#0.4#> So yes, your head really is older than your feet. By about half a millionth of a second, over your whole life.
